histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What type of epithelium lines the oesophagus?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium — built to resist mechanical abrasion from the food bolus.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Why is the oesophageal epithelium stratified squamous rather than columnar?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: It is a protective, non-absorptive conduit; a thick multilayered squamous lining resists abrasion from passing food.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Is the surface epithelium of the oesophagus keratinised?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: No — it is non-keratinised, so the flattened surface cells still retain their nuclei (unlike skin).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: List the four layers of the oesophageal (and general GI) wall from the lumen outward.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Mucosa → submucosa → muscularis externa → adventitia (or serosa).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What single feature best distinguishes the oesophagus from other stratified-squamous-lined organs on a slide?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Mucous glands (oesophageal glands proper) sitting in the submucosa — few other sites have submucosal glands.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What are the three components of the mucosa?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Epithelium, lamina propria, and muscularis mucosae.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Where are the oesophageal glands proper located and what do they secrete?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: In the submucosa, along the whole length; they are tubuloacinar mucous glands that secrete mucus to lubricate the bolus.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Where are the oesophageal cardiac glands located?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: In the lamina propria at the two ends of the oesophagus (near the pharynx and near the stomach); they are mucous glands.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: How do you tell the two named oesophageal glands apart?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Cardiac glands = lamina propria, at the ends; glands proper = submucosa, whole length.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is unusual about the muscularis mucosae of the oesophagus?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: It is thick and mostly longitudinal (thicker than in most of the gut), and thickens distally toward the stomach.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is found in the submucosa besides glands?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Dense irregular connective tissue with larger blood vessels, lymphatics, the Meissner (submucosal) nerve plexus, and a longitudinal venous plexus.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Which nerve plexus lies in the submucosa and what does it control?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: The Meissner (submucosal) plexus — it controls glandular secretion and local blood flow.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What are the two muscle layers of the muscularis externa and their orientation?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Inner circular and outer longitudinal.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What muscle type forms the muscularis externa in the upper third of the oesophagus?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Skeletal (striated) muscle — the voluntary start of swallowing.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What muscle type forms the muscularis externa in the middle third?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Mixed skeletal and smooth muscle.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What muscle type forms the muscularis externa in the lower third?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Smooth muscle — involuntary peristalsis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Which nerve plexus lies between the two muscularis externa layers and what does it do?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus — it drives peristalsis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What kind of muscle forms the upper oesophageal sphincter?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Skeletal muscle (the cricopharyngeus).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is the nature of the lower oesophageal sphincter?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: A physiological (functional) smooth-muscle sphincter, reinforced by the crura of the diaphragm; not a discrete anatomical thickening.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Does the oesophagus have an adventitia or a serosa?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Mostly adventitia (no mesothelial covering); only the short abdominal segment below the diaphragm has a true serosa.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Why does the lack of a serosa matter clinically?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Without a serosal barrier, oesophageal tumours spread locally early and perforations leak into the mediastinum — contributing to poor prognosis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is the Z-line?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: The squamocolumnar junction at the gastro-oesophageal junction — the abrupt change from stratified squamous to gastric simple columnar epithelium.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is Barrett's oesophagus?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Metaplasia of the oesophageal stratified squamous epithelium into columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia), driven by chronic acid reflux.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Why is Barrett's oesophagus important?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: It is premalignant — the main risk factor for oesophageal adenocarcinoma; monitored with surveillance endoscopy/biopsy for dysplasia.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What are the histological features of reflux oesophagitis?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Basal cell hyperplasia, elongated lamina-propria papillae, and intra-epithelial eosinophils and neutrophils.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Where does oesophageal adenocarcinoma arise and what is its main risk factor?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: In the lower third, from Barrett's oesophagus; risk factors are GORD and obesity. It is the commonest type in the West.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Where does oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma arise and what are its risk factors?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: In the upper/middle third; risk factors are smoking and alcohol. It is the commonest type worldwide.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What are oesophageal varices and where do they form?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Dilated submucosal veins at the distal oesophagus, caused by portal hypertension (a porto-systemic anastomosis); a cause of massive upper-GI bleeding.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is the histological basis of achalasia?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus of the lower oesophagus → failure of LOS relaxation and loss of peristalsis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What defines eosinophilic oesophagitis histologically?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: More than 15 eosinophils per high-power field in the epithelium, with endoscopic rings and furrows; typically young atopic patients with dysphagia.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: Why is the oesophageal lumen star-shaped in cross-section?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: Longitudinal mucosal and submucosal folds project into the lumen at rest and flatten out when a bolus passes.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.front: What is a Mallory–Weiss tear?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.back: A mucosal laceration at the gastro-oesophageal junction after forceful vomiting/retching, causing haematemesis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is the main function of the stomach?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: To mix food and secrete acid and enzymes, beginning protein digestion and converting the bolus into chyme.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What type of surface epithelium lines the stomach?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Simple columnar epithelium (surface mucous cells) that dips down into gastric pits.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is a gastric pit (foveola)?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: An invagination of the surface epithelium into which the gastric glands empty; the pit is lined by surface mucous cells.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Which two features tell you a slide is stomach and NOT intestine?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Absence of goblet cells and absence of villi (the stomach has gastric pits and a flat surface instead).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Name the four regions of the stomach.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus (antrum).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Which regions contain the oxyntic (gastric) glands and what do they make?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: The fundus and body; their glands contain parietal and chief cells and produce acid and pepsinogen.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What characterises the pyloric/antral mucosa histologically?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Deep gastric pits overlying short, coiled mucous glands, rich in G cells; few or no parietal cells.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: List the layers of the pit–gland unit from surface to base.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Gastric pit (foveola) → isthmus/neck (stem cells + mucous neck cells) → gland body and base (parietal, chief, enteroendocrine cells).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Where are the gastric stem cells located?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: In the isthmus/neck of the gland; they renew the epithelium upward into the pit and downward into the gland.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What do surface and neck mucous cells secrete?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Bicarbonate-rich (alkaline) mucus that protects the mucosa from acid and abrasion.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Describe the appearance of parietal cells on H&E.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Large, rounded, eosinophilic (pink) 'fried-egg' cells with a central nucleus, located in the upper/mid gland.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What do parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Hydrochloric acid (via the H+/K+ ATPase proton pump) and intrinsic factor.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Describe the appearance of chief cells on H&E.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Basophilic (blue) basal cytoplasm (abundant RER) with apical zymogen granules; located at the gland base.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What do chief (zymogenic) cells secrete?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Pepsinogen (activated to pepsin by acid) and gastric lipase.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Where in the gland are parietal vs chief cells concentrated?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Parietal cells are higher up (upper/mid gland); chief cells are deeper, at the gland base.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is the mnemonic for parietal vs chief cell staining?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: 'Parietal Pink, Chief Chromatic-blue' — parietal cells are eosinophilic, chief cells are basophilic.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Which cell secretes intrinsic factor, and why does it matter?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: The parietal cell; intrinsic factor binds vitamin B12 for absorption in the terminal ileum. Loss of parietal cells causes B12 deficiency.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Which enteroendocrine cell secretes gastrin and where is it found?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: The G cell, found mainly in the antrum/pylorus.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Which cell secretes histamine to stimulate acid, and which secretes somatostatin to inhibit it?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: ECL cells secrete histamine (stimulates parietal cells via H2 receptors); D cells secrete somatostatin (inhibits acid).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is the final common step of acid secretion and which drug targets it?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: The H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) on parietal-cell canaliculi; targeted by proton pump inhibitors (PPIs).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What three stimuli increase parietal-cell acid secretion?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Gastrin (G cells), histamine (ECL cells, via H2 receptors), and acetylcholine (vagus).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What inhibits gastric acid secretion?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Somatostatin from D cells; low luminal pH also switches off gastrin release (negative feedback).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What are the components of the gastric mucosal barrier?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: The mucus–bicarbonate layer, surface epithelial tight junctions, prostaglandin-maintained mucus and blood flow, and rapid epithelial turnover.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: How do NSAIDs cause gastric ulcers?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: They inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, weakening the protective mucus/bicarbonate barrier and mucosal blood flow, leading to erosions and ulcers.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: How many muscle layers does the gastric muscularis externa have, and what is the extra one?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Three layers — an extra inner oblique layer in addition to the middle circular and outer longitudinal layers, enabling churning.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What causes H. pylori-associated gastritis and its complications?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Curved Gram-negative bacilli colonise the antral mucus layer, causing chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, MALT lymphoma, and adenocarcinoma.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is autoimmune (atrophic) gastritis and its consequences?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Autoantibodies against parietal cells and intrinsic factor destroy parietal cells (body/fundus) → achlorhydria and pernicious anaemia (B12 deficiency).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is intestinal metaplasia of the stomach and why does it matter?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Replacement of gastric epithelium by intestinal-type epithelium with goblet cells; it is a premalignant change toward gastric adenocarcinoma.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Contrast the two histological types of gastric adenocarcinoma.
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: Intestinal type forms glands and arises on metaplasia; diffuse type has signet-ring cells, causes linitis plastica, and shows E-cadherin (CDH1) loss.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is Zollinger–Ellison syndrome?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: A gastrin-secreting tumour (gastrinoma) that drives parietal-cell hyperplasia, excess acid, and multiple/refractory peptic ulcers.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: What is a GIST and its key marker?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: A gastrointestinal stromal tumour from the interstitial cells of Cajal; positive for c-KIT (CD117).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.front: Why does the circular muscle layer thicken at the gastric outlet?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.back: It forms the pyloric sphincter, controlling emptying of chyme into the duodenum.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: The epithelium lining the lumen of the oesophagus is:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: The oesophagus is lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, adapted to resist abrasion by the food bolus.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: On a slide, which feature most reliably identifies tissue as oesophagus?
options: Goblet cells in the surface epithelium
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: Oesophageal glands proper lie in the submucosa. Submucosal glands are found in only a few sites (oesophagus and the duodenal Brunner glands), making them a strong discriminator.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: The muscularis externa in the upper third of the oesophagus is composed of:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: The upper third is skeletal muscle, the middle third is mixed, and the lower third is smooth muscle.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: The muscularis externa of the lower third of the oesophagus is composed of:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: The lower third is smooth muscle, mediating involuntary peristalsis. Skeletal is upper, mixed is middle.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: The oesophageal glands proper are located in the:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: The oesophageal glands proper are mucous glands in the submucosa along the whole length; the cardiac glands (at the two ends) sit in the lamina propria.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: Oesophageal varices form from dilated veins in which layer?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: Varices are dilated veins of the submucosal (porto-systemic) venous plexus in the distal oesophagus, occurring in portal hypertension.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: Barrett's oesophagus is best described as:
options: Metaplasia of squamous to columnar epithelium with goblet cells
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: Barrett's is intestinal metaplasia — squamous epithelium replaced by columnar epithelium containing goblet cells — caused by chronic reflux, and is premalignant.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: Achalasia results from the loss of ganglion cells in the:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: Achalasia is degeneration of the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus of the lower oesophagus, causing a non-relaxing LOS and absent peristalsis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: The Z-line refers to:
options: The junction between mucosa and submucosa
The abrupt squamous-to-columnar epithelial junction at the GOJ
The line of the muscularis mucosae
The transition from skeletal to smooth muscle
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: The Z-line (squamocolumnar junction) marks the abrupt change from oesophageal stratified squamous to gastric simple columnar epithelium.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: Oesophageal adenocarcinoma characteristically arises:
options: In the upper third, related to smoking
In the lower third, from Barrett's oesophagus
In the middle third, from achalasia
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: Adenocarcinoma arises in the lower third from Barrett's metaplasia (GORD/obesity), and is the commonest oesophageal cancer in the West.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is located:
options: Between the inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle layers
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: The myenteric plexus lies between the two muscularis externa layers and coordinates peristalsis; the submucosal (Meissner) plexus controls secretion.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: Over most of its length the outer coat of the oesophagus is:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: Most of the oesophagus is covered by adventitia; only the short abdominal segment has a true serosa. This favours early local tumour spread.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: Which histological features suggest reflux oesophagitis?
options: Basal cell hyperplasia, elongated papillae and intra-epithelial eosinophils
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: Reflux oesophagitis shows basal cell hyperplasia, elongated lamina-propria papillae, and intra-epithelial eosinophils/neutrophils.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: Oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma is most associated with:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: SCC (upper/middle third, commonest worldwide) is linked to smoking and alcohol; adenocarcinoma is the Barrett's/GORD-related lower-third tumour.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: The muscularis mucosae of the oesophagus is notable for being:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: The oesophageal muscularis mucosae is unusually thick and predominantly longitudinal, thickening toward the stomach.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: The upper oesophageal sphincter is formed by:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: The UOS is skeletal muscle (cricopharyngeus). The LOS is a physiological smooth-muscle sphincter aided by the diaphragmatic crura.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: The oesophageal cardiac glands differ from the glands proper in that they:
options: Lie in the lamina propria at the two ends of the oesophagus
Are found only in the middle third
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: Cardiac glands are mucous glands in the lamina propria at the two ends; the glands proper are mucous glands in the submucosa along the whole length.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is diagnosed histologically by:
options: More than 15 eosinophils per high-power field
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: Eosinophilic oesophagitis requires >15 intra-epithelial eosinophils/hpf, with endoscopic rings and furrows, typically in young atopic patients.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus of the oesophagus primarily controls:
options: Peristaltic contraction of the muscularis externa
Glandular secretion and local blood flow
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus regulates glandular secretion and local blood flow; the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus drives muscle peristalsis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.question: A Mallory–Weiss tear is:
options: A full-thickness perforation of the mid-oesophagus
A mucosal laceration at the GOJ after forceful vomiting
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Oesophagus.explanation: A Mallory–Weiss tear is a mucosal laceration at the gastro-oesophageal junction following forceful vomiting/retching, presenting with haematemesis.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: The surface epithelium of the stomach is:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: The stomach is lined by simple columnar epithelium (surface mucous cells) that dips into gastric pits.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: Which feature distinguishes gastric mucosa from small-intestinal mucosa?
options: Absence of goblet cells and villi
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: Gastric mucosa has gastric pits but no goblet cells and no villi; goblet cells/villi indicate intestine (or intestinal metaplasia).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: Parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: Parietal cells secrete HCl (via the H+/K+ ATPase) and intrinsic factor. Pepsinogen is from chief cells.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: Chief (zymogenic) cells are recognised on H&E as:
options: Eosinophilic 'fried-egg' cells high in the gland
Basophilic cells with apical granules at the gland base
Pale mucous cells at the surface
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: Chief cells have basophilic basal cytoplasm (RER) and apical zymogen granules, sitting deep at the gland base; they secrete pepsinogen.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: Intrinsic factor, required for vitamin B12 absorption, is secreted by:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: Parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor as well as acid; loss of parietal cells causes B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia).

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: Gastrin is produced by which cell, located mainly in which region?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: G cells of the antrum/pylorus secrete gastrin, which stimulates acid secretion.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: The final common step of gastric acid secretion, and the target of PPIs, is:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: The parietal-cell H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) is the final step of acid secretion and the target of proton pump inhibitors.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: Which cell secretes histamine to stimulate parietal-cell acid production?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: Enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells release histamine, which stimulates parietal cells via H2 receptors.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: Somatostatin, which inhibits gastric acid secretion, is released by:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: D cells secrete somatostatin, inhibiting acid secretion and gastrin release.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: Which glands and cell types predominate in the body and fundus of the stomach?
options: Oxyntic glands with parietal and chief cells
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: The body and fundus contain oxyntic (gastric) glands rich in parietal and chief cells, producing acid and pepsinogen.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: The gastric muscularis externa is distinctive because it has:
options: Two layers like the rest of the gut
Three layers, with an extra inner oblique layer
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: The stomach has three muscle layers — inner oblique, middle circular, outer longitudinal — the extra oblique layer aiding churning.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: NSAIDs predispose to gastric ulcers primarily by:
options: Inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis and weakening the mucosal barrier
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase/prostaglandins, reducing protective mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow, promoting ulceration.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: Autoimmune (atrophic) gastritis characteristically causes:
options: Loss of parietal cells with achlorhydria and pernicious anaemia
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: Antibodies to parietal cells and intrinsic factor destroy parietal cells (body/fundus), causing achlorhydria and B12-deficient pernicious anaemia.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: The appearance of goblet cells within the gastric mucosa indicates:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: Goblet cells are not normally present in the stomach; their appearance is intestinal metaplasia, a step toward adenocarcinoma.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma is characterised by:

Signet-ring cells and linitis plastica with E-cadherin loss

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: Helicobacter pylori is classically associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: Pernicious anaemia is caused by autoimmune gastritis, not H. pylori. H. pylori causes gastritis, ulcers, MALT lymphoma and adenocarcinoma.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: Zollinger–Ellison syndrome results from a tumour secreting:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: A gastrinoma secretes excess gastrin, driving parietal-cell hyperplasia, high acid output and multiple/refractory ulcers.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: GISTs arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal and are characteristically c-KIT (CD117) positive.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: Which cells provide the alkaline mucus of the gastric mucosal barrier?
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: Surface and mucous neck cells secrete bicarbonate-rich mucus that protects the epithelium from acid.

histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.question: The gastric stem cells that renew the epithelium reside in the:
histology__GASTROINTESTINAL__Stomach (la.explanation: Stem cells lie in the isthmus/neck, renewing cells upward into the pit and downward into the gland.
